title: Son of the Bride
full_review:
A mild heart attack causes a divorced restauranteur to reevaluate his life in the slice-of-life tale "Son of the Bride" (Sony Pictures Classics).

Overwhelmed and completely stressed out, 42-year-old Rafael (Ricardo Darin) is having a melt down. He can't get his suppliers to deliver goods to his restaurant because the bank hasn't cleared his check. His ex-wife Sandra (Claudia Fontan) is constantly nagging him about playing a bigger role in their daughter Vicky's (Gimena Nobile) life. He's so wrapped up in himself and his problems that he can't make a commitment to his beautiful young girlfriend Nati (Natalia Verbeke). And to top things off his old childhood chum Juan Carlos (Eduardo Blanco) has re-entered his life and wants to make up for lost time.

Director Juan Jose Campanella has created a dynamic story set in Argentina with strong, believable characters about responsibility, fulfillment, atonement and moving on in life. Rafael is a typical, middle-class Joe who is struggling to make everything work. When his father Nino (Hector Alterio), an Italian immigrant who founded the restaurant, announces that he's decided to fulfill his mother's dream of getting married in a church, Rafael cannot share in Nino's happiness. After 44 years of marriage, with his mother Norma in a nursing home suffering from Alzheimer's, what's the point? And hidden deep within Rafael's heart is a bitter resentment against his mother for making him feel like a failure when he quit law school to enter the restaurant business.

Campanella uses the comedic drama to comment on the political and economic crises in Argentina. Just when he needs them most, the institutions that might help Rafael fail him. The bank won't give him the money he needs to pay his suppliers -- and stay in business -- which is linked to the decline in the country's economy. He finally comes around to the idea of a church wedding for his parents (after a heart attack forces some much needed self-reflection), and the local pastor refuses to marry them because Norma not mentally capable to take the vows.

Rafael's journey from self-involved to rueful to lover of life is captured in reflections -- his image is seen in mirrors, windows, a glass table, a television set. Campanella uses these images as a metaphor for reflecting on life and all it has to offer. But it is the convincing rapport between the characters that is the grease that keeps this film going. And Juan Carlos is the linchpin of the story. He is held up as the ideal person, suffering a great tragedy, sinking to the ultimate depths of despair, and then cleaning up his act and maintaining a positive attitude.

Through him, Rafael comes to see how good his own life is and how much he has to be thankful for, not how much he has to complain about.

The representation of the Church as cold-hearted doesn't seem to be intended to single it out as much as to say it is just another place where Rafael doesn't find help. As a Catholic viewer, one is likely to understand that situations such as Nino and Norma's wouldn't be seen as black and white as they are presented here. Unfortunately, though, the film ends with Juan Carlos, who dabbles in acting, playing a priest administering the sacrament of marriage to the couple.

Ultimately, Rafael discovers that in his struggle to be someone important, he has overlooked that fact that he already is: a son, a father and a friend. With heart-warming moments as well as hearty laughs, "Son of the Bride" reflects on the importance of appreciating life here and now.

Due to the impersonation of a priest administering the sacrament of marriage, fleeting drug use and rear nudity and recurring rough language with profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
